q: Does the graph-transformer GNN's expressibility-prediction accuracy (paper: RMSE 0.05 up to n=10) hold when extrapolating to large-scale PQC ansätze with 100s–1000s of qubits, where barren-plateau physics dominates and per-PQC training data becomes prohibitive?
basis: Paper's largest reported extrapolation is n≤5 → n=10 (Fig 11). Our replication saw per-qubit RMSE degrade monotonically from 0.33 at n=3 to 0.72 at n=6, i.e. accuracy worsens at the edge of the training distribution. Beyond ~30–50 qubits, exact statevector KL ground truth becomes computationally intractable (Hilbert dim 2^n), so the model must be trained on approximate or surrogate targets — a regime the paper never enters. Independently, PQCs in this size range are known to enter barren-plateau regimes where expressibility saturates near a 2-design; the fidelity distribution collapses toward Haar and KL → 0, which may make the regression target degenerate.
next_steps: Design a synthetic ground-truth target valid at large n (e.g. analytic frame-potential moments for restricted PQC families instead of empirical KL from 5000 samples).
Sweep n = 8, 12, 16, 24, 32 with matched-architecture PQCs and measure per-n RMSE and per-n Pearson r on held-out ansätze.

Quantify the barren-plateau gradient variance for the tested large-n ansätze alongside GNN-predicted expressibility, to establish whether the GNN target itself becomes an ill-conditioned regression problem.
Test few-shot / transfer-learning strategies: pretrain the GNN on small-n statevector-KL then fine-tune on large-n proxy metrics (e.g. shadow-fidelity, classical-shadow expressibility estimators).

q: Does the GNN-predicted expressibility correlate (or anti-correlate) with actual downstream task performance — VQE ground-state energy error, QML classification accuracy, generative-model quality — across chemistry, combinatorial-optimisation, and QML problem families?
basis: The paper defines and predicts expressibility as an intrinsic geometric property of the PQC (KL-divergence to Haar) but does not connect it to end-task utility. The literature is mixed: Holmes et al. (2022) show high-expressibility ansätze often suffer barren plateaus (anti-correlation with trainability); Sim et al. (2019) posit expressibility as loosely correlated with representational capacity; problem-informed ansätze (UCCSD, HVA, QAOA) can be low-expressibility yet high-performing on their target Hamiltonian. Our replication tested only the intrinsic KL target, not any downstream task.
next_steps: Build a benchmark suite: 3 chemistry Hamiltonians (H2, LiH, BeH2), 3 MaxCut instances, 3 QML classification tasks (Iris, moons, MNIST-2-class subset).

For each of ~200 random PQC ansätze per task, run both the GNN expressibility predictor and the full task-training loop; report Spearman rank correlation between GNN-predicted expressibility and final task loss.
Stratify by problem family and by ansatz depth to test whether correlation flips sign in different regimes (e.g. positive in shallow QML, negative in deep VQE due to barren-plateau interference).
Compare against a task-conditioned GNN variant that takes the target Hamiltonian graph as an auxiliary input.

q: Is the paper's noise-aware GNN (trained on three fake noisy IBM backends, RMSE 0.06) actually robust enough to rank real NISQ-hardware ansätze correctly, when the deployment device's noise profile differs from all training backends?
basis: Paper trains on FakeGuadalupe/Mumbai/Hanoi (Claim C6) and reports a single Table I hardware-vs-predicted comparison on IBM-Hanoi (e.g. Circuit 3 hardware KL 0.280 vs predicted 0.402). One data point on the same-name fake-backend twin is not evidence of cross-device generalisation. Our replication skipped noisy experiments entirely (out-of-scope), so we cannot even reproduce the single Hanoi point, let alone evaluate noise-transfer.
next_steps: Reproduce the noise-aware pipeline: expand node features to 23 dims with per-qubit T1, T2, gate error, readout error from Qiskit fake-backend calibration.
Train on backends A,B and test on held-out backend C; repeat for all leave-one-out splits across ≥6 fake backends spanning heavy-hex and linear-chain topologies.
Run a small hardware campaign (~20 circuits × 2 real IBM devices) and measure Kendall-tau ranking agreement between GNN prediction and hardware-measured KL.
Test domain-adaptation methods (adversarial features, MMD alignment) to close the sim-to-real noise gap.

q: Would a hybrid architecture augmenting the graph topology with physics-informed features (KAK-decomposition rank, distance-to-nearest-2-design via frame potential, quantum Fisher information trace) outperform the pure graph-topology-plus-count-statistics model on both accuracy and interpretability?
basis: Paper's global-feature branch uses only 13 count-style statistics (depth, n_params, per-gate counts). Our replication reproduced this baseline and observed the worst Sim-19 misses on Circuits 9, 17, 19 — structurally atypical circuits whose expressibility is driven by algebraic properties (Circuit 9 is pure H+CZ+RX, has near-zero parameterised gates yet high KL) that count-statistics cannot capture. Physics-informed features like KAK are cheap to compute for small blocks and provide direct algebraic signal about SU(4) coverage.
next_steps: Implement three feature sets: (a) baseline paper features, (b) baseline + KAK-per-two-qubit-block invariants, (c) baseline + Fisher-information-trace estimate + shadow-frame-potential estimate.
Ablate: full GNN, GNN + (a), GNN + (b), GNN + (c), globals-only-MLP with (c). Report RMSE and Pearson r on both random hold-out and Sim-19.
Use SHAP or integrated-gradients attribution on the global-feature branch to test whether physics features receive higher attribution weight on the previously-worst-predicted circuits (9, 17, 19).
Measure per-feature compute overhead to characterise the accuracy–cost trade-off for practical ansatz-search deployment.

q: Can the GNN expressibility predictor be integrated as a fast fitness/reward oracle inside reinforcement-learning or evolutionary quantum-architecture-search loops to yield automated ansatz designs that outperform hand-crafted baselines across chemistry, optimisation, and QML — with results reproducible across quantum SDKs (Qiskit, Pennylane, Cirq, TKET) and hardware backends?
basis: Paper's stated motivation is that classical KL estimation (5000 samples per PQC) is a bottleneck for ansatz search. A GNN inference is orders of magnitude faster than statevector sampling, so it is naturally suited as an inner-loop fitness oracle. But the paper never closes this loop: no search experiment, no comparison to random search or Bayesian optimisation, no cross-SDK portability test. Reproducibility across SDKs matters because gate decompositions and default synthesis differ (e.g. Qiskit's CZ vs Pennylane's CZ vs Cirq's CZPowGate all target the same unitary but produce different circuit graphs), potentially breaking any GNN trained on a single SDK's serialised form.
next_steps: Wrap the trained GNN as a fitness function; run an evolutionary search (NSGA-II) and a PPO agent over a fixed gate library, budget-matched against random search.
Evaluate discovered ansätze on VQE (H2/LiH), QAOA (MaxCut), and QML (moons) tasks; report Pareto front of expressibility vs task performance.
Cross-SDK: retrain the GNN on circuits generated in Pennylane and Cirq, and cross-evaluate predictions across all three SDKs to measure prediction-invariance under gate-vocabulary re-encoding.

Deploy top-k ansätze on ≥2 real hardware backends (IBM heavy-hex, IonQ trapped-ion) and report end-task metric variance vs GNN-predicted expressibility ranking — closing the loop from search-oracle to deployed hardware result.
